summary: Jon Postel gives three suggestions for detecting messages lost by the network's communications subsystem. The first is for a host to keep a copy of each message until the network says it was delivered, and to resend it with a limit on retries if the network reports an incomplete transmission.

eli5.summary: Keep a copy of every letter you send until you hear it arrived, and send it again if it did not.

subtitle: Jon Postel offers three ways for a host to notice that the network has lost a message.

tldr.problem: The communications subsystem could lose messages, and hosts had no systematic way of noticing.
tldr.mechanism: Three schemes: keep a copy of each message until the network answers and resend on INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION, number messages per host pair so gaps show up, or add host-to-host acknowledgments.
tldr.outcome: The first scheme is called the most immediately practical, and several hosts already did it. The schemes do not conflict, so they could be used together.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 516 as Unknown, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. RFC 512 builds on its second scheme.

sections.title: Three Suggestions
sections.content: Jonathan Postel of UCLA-NMC offers three suggestions for detecting the loss of messages by the communications subsystem. He calls the first perhaps the most powerful and simplest to implement, since it uses no new concepts and can retransmit a message detected as lost.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to be sure your mail got there: keep a copy, number the letters, or ask for a receipt.

sections.title: Scheme One: Save a Copy and Wait
sections.content:
After sending a message, the host saves a copy and waits for the network's reply. A RFNM means all is well and the next message is processed. An INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION means the copy is retransmitted, with a finite upper bound on retries since it could loop. A DESTINATION DEAD means the destination is marked down and a reset exchange is required before more communication.

Anything else indicates an error in the network or local IMP, so it should at least be logged and probably the conversation closed. This can be done per host or per link.
sections.eli5: Hold on to your copy until the post office says delivered. If it says it fell out of the truck, send the copy again, but not forever.

sections.title: Schemes Two and Three: Numbers and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
In the second scheme, message numbers go in the host to host header, per host pair. Messages must be delivered in order, which the network does except for priority messages, so each host would send everything or nothing as priority. Resets set the numbers between a pair of hosts to zero. The sender puts the current number in the header and increments it modulo N (for example N=256). The receiver compares the arriving number with the expected one; a mismatch means a message was lost.

What to do on a gap is not clear, but it can be logged and reported to the network control center. Unrecovered missing messages should close the conversation, since loss may be tolerable in interactive use but is critical in file transfer.

The third scheme would require host to host acknowledgments, similar to the IMP to IMP scheme. This is a serious change to current protocols, so Postel does not elaborate.
sections.eli5: Number every letter so gaps show, or have the other side send back a receipt for each one. The receipt idea is the biggest change, so it is left for later.

items.title: 1. Save and resend
items.text: Keep a copy until RFNM; resend on INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSION.

items.title: 2. Message numbers
items.text: Per host pair numbering in the host to host header, checked on receipt.

items.title: 3. Host acknowledgments
items.text: Host to host acks, a serious protocol change left for further study.
